claims.text: Large-scale atomistic simulations with explicit 1 wt.% oxygen defects will predict the thermal conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than existing analytical models.
The claimed accuracy improvement applies in both the near-0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The target material is fully dense, polycrystalline bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The simulation will explicitly represent randomly distributed oxygen defects, lattice disorder, and temperature-dependent phonon scattering.
Literature thermal-conductivity measurements exist over approximately 0–200 K and 300–1200 K for HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen occurs as randomly dispersed interstitials that produce local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Local lattice distortions and defects scatter phonons.
Oxygen-induced distortions scatter phonons throughout the full near-0–1200 K range.
Explicit treatment of non-ideal defect structures captures phonon-scattering pathways neglected by analytical approaches.
Capturing those defect-related scattering pathways will improve agreement with measurements on oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
Predicted thermal conductivities will differ from experiment by less than 10–15%.
The defect-aware simulation will improve predictive accuracy by at least a factor of two relative to continuum or perfect-crystal phenomenological models.
Existing analytical models are restricted to perfect crystals and exclude oxygen defects.
Existing analytical models typically have errors exceeding 25% for real HfNbTaTiZr samples.
The approach is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr containing no more than 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–1200 K.
Its parameterization is uncertain above 1 wt.% oxygen or above 1200 K.
Oxygen-vacancy clustering, secondary-phase formation, or departure from a random defect distribution could increase prediction errors beyond the stated range.
Thermal conductivity will be benchmarked using measured diffusivity, specific heat, and density on specimens verified to contain 1 wt.% oxygen.
A deviation greater than 15% in either temperature regime will falsify the stated accuracy hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The design specifies cryogenic measurements from 10 K to 150 K, whereas the measurement specification says to focus on 10–200 K.
